# Experimental Design

## Obtaining good data, and anticipating what will go wrong before it does {.unnumbered}

::: {.column-margin .margin-legend}
**Margin legend**

**DEF** — definition **KEY** — key idea to remember **↪** — bridge to another lecture **⚠** — common pitfall
:::

## Where this chapter fits

This chapter comes straight after *Why statistics?*, and before any machine-learning method is introduced. It has been established that a statistical model is a crude approximation of a complicated process. Everything here is directed at one practical goal: arriving at data whose structure is understood, so that the subsequent analysis is sound rather than hopeful. A machine-learning method is at least as dependent on this as a classical test, and it is far less likely to warn you when the data were badly collected.

The lecture is framed by a warning that should be kept in mind throughout:

> "To consult the statistician after an experiment is finished is often merely to ask him to conduct a post mortem examination. He can perhaps say what the experiment died of."
>
> — Sir Ronald Aylmer Fisher

Fisher's point is that most of the leverage over a study is spent *before* a single measurement is taken. Once the data exist, their quality is fixed and constrains the model; the analysis can only reveal it, not repair it. This chapter therefore concerns the decisions made early, and a vocabulary — type I and type II error, power, the experimental unit — that allows those decisions to be reasoned about precisely.

Some of what follows may appear almost too simple. That is intentional. These "obvious" ideas are exactly the ones whose quiet violation produces the subtle failures that the remainder of the course is devoted to detecting and correcting.

Four principles underlie the whole lecture:

- In confirmatory research the hypothesis chooses the method and the data. In exploratory research and in prediction the order is reversed, and the design must protect against that reversal.
- A good method or model yields an **unambiguous** decision about the hypothesis.
- Any statement about a hypothesis is a statement about random variables — a statement in terms of *probability*, never certainty.
- Errors propagate forward. A poor research question cannot be repaired by good statistics, and poor data cannot be repaired by a clever model.

## Three kinds of question

Before any design decision, one question has to be answered: *what kind of question is this study asking?* The course meets three kinds, and they differ in the order in which hypothesis and data arrive.

- **Confirming a hypothesis.** The hypothesis comes first and chooses the data: what to measure, on whom, how many. The study ends with a test, and a well-designed, randomised study may say that the treatment *causes* the effect. This is the world of Day 1 and of most of this chapter.
- **Exploring data to generate hypotheses.** The data come first, often measured on thousands of genes at once, and the analysis looks for structure: groups of patients, directions of variation, modules of co-expressed genes. What comes out is a *hypothesis*, not a conclusion. This is the world of PCA and clustering (Days 4 and 5).
- **Predicting an outcome.** The aim is neither to test nor to explain, but to predict a label or a value for new cases: tumour or normal, responder or not. Success is measured by the error on cases the model has never seen, and nothing is claimed about mechanism. This is the world of Days 6 to 11.

::: column-margin
**DEF** — **Hypothesis-driven** (confirmatory) research lets the hypothesis select the data. **Data-driven** (exploratory) research lets the data select the hypothesis.
:::





::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Code for the diagram"}
box <- function(x, y, label, fill = "white", border = "grey30") {
  rect(x - 0.7, y - 0.28, x + 0.7, y + 0.28, col = fill, border = border, lwd = 1.5)
  text(x, y, label, cex = 0.8)
}
chain <- function(y, labels, fills, title) {
  xs <- seq(1.5, by = 1.8, length.out = length(labels))
  text(0, y, title, adj = 0, font = 2, cex = 0.85)
  for (k in seq_along(labels)) box(xs[k], y, labels[k], fills[k])
  if (length(xs) > 1) arrows(xs[-length(xs)] + 0.72, y, xs[-1] - 0.72, y, length = 0.07, lwd = 1.5)
}
new <- "#F6D7C3"; plain <- "white"
par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 9.6), ylim = c(0.4, 3.6), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
chain(3.1, c("hypothesis", "design", "new data", "test"), c(plain, plain, new, plain), "Confirm")
chain(2.0, c("data", "pattern", "hypothesis", "new data", "test"), c(plain, plain, plain, new, plain), "Explore")
chain(0.9, c("data", "model", "new data", "error"), c(plain, plain, new, plain), "Predict")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Three kinds of question, read from left to right. The orange box marks where data that played no part in forming the hypothesis or building the model enter. In confirmatory research these are the data of the study itself, because the hypothesis was fixed beforehand. In exploration and prediction they have to be new data, and that has to be designed in.](02-design_files/figure-html/fig-three-questions-1.png){#fig-three-questions width=816}
:::
:::





The diagram shows why the distinction matters for design. A *p*-value, a confidence interval or an error rate is only honest when it is computed on data that played no part in choosing what is being tested. In confirmatory research this is guaranteed by the order of events: the hypothesis was fixed before the data existed. In exploration and prediction the order is reversed. A pattern found in a data set will always look convincing *in that data set*, because that is why it was found. The independent data have to come from somewhere else, and that "somewhere else" must be planned before the study starts.

The three kinds of question also license different claims. A randomised experiment may claim a cause; an exploratory analysis may claim only that something is worth testing; a predictive model may claim an error rate on a stated population, and nothing about why it works [@Shmueli2010; @Breiman2001].

::: column-margin
**KEY** — A hypothesis cannot be tested on the data that suggested it. Exploration and prediction are as dependent on design as a confirmatory test; the design simply has to provide something else.
:::

Most of this chapter treats the confirmatory case, because its vocabulary (experimental unit, randomisation, blocking, power) is needed for everything else. The section [When the data come first](#sec-data-first) then shows what changes, and what does not, when the data come before the hypothesis.

::: {.callout-caution title="Check yourself"}
Classify each study as confirmatory, exploratory or predictive. (a) RNA-seq of 200 breast tumours, to find out whether there are subtypes not yet described. (b) A randomised trial of a drug against placebo, with blood pressure after eight weeks as the outcome. (c) A model that uses methylation at 500 CpG sites to tell whether a biopsy contains tumour cells.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
(a) is exploratory: the subtypes are the result, and they are hypotheses until confirmed in other tumours. (b) is confirmatory: the hypothesis was fixed in advance, the treatment is randomised, and the trial ends in a test. (c) is predictive: the question is how often the model is right on new biopsies, not which CpG sites cause cancer. Real projects often combine the three; the design must say which part answers which kind of question.
:::
:::
## From data to facts

The purpose of an experiment is to turn measurements into a defensible claim about the world — to convert **data into facts**. That conversion succeeds only if a chain of earlier decisions was made well. The chain is set out explicitly, because each link is a place at which the whole argument can quietly fail:

- **Input.** Everything begins with a research question. If it is vague, nothing downstream can sharpen it.
- **Population.** The objects the question concerns must be identified — humans of a certain sex, age and location; a plant species under certain conditions. The population is a definition, and the researcher is responsible for it.
- **Data acquisition.** The sample must represent the population's properties faithfully. This is where representativeness is won or lost.
- **Sample size.** The sample must be large enough to detect the effect of interest. Later in this chapter "large enough" becomes a computable quantity.
- **Confounders.** Effects that were not intended for study but which nonetheless move the response must be compensated for.
- **Reproducibility.** The acquisition process itself must be repeatable — by the same researcher later, and ideally by someone else entirely.
- **Quality, twice over.** The quality of the data depends critically on the acquisition process; that quality in turn bounds the complexity and trustworthiness of every subsequent analysis.

The last point is the through-line of the lecture. Data quality is not a property assessed at the end; it is designed in at the start, or it is absent.

## A model is where experimental design begins

For a confirmatory study, the idea that connects this lecture to the first one is the following: before any pipette or field is touched, the hypothesis of interest is translated into a model to be fitted. For a study of blood pressure, for example:

$$\text{Bloodpressure} \sim \text{Gender} + \text{Concentration} + \text{Time of day}$$

This single line is already a design document. Read carefully, it conveys a surprising amount:

- **It states what is to be measured.** Every term is a column that must be recorded.
- **It states the data types**, and therefore the measurement method for each. Gender is nominal, concentration numerical, time of day ordinal or numerical, and the response numerical. Knowing the type is knowing how the variable will be measured.
- **It states where variance will enter.** Every measurement method has an accuracy, and every accuracy is a source of variance. That variance may be of no scientific interest, but if the factor driving it is *recorded*, it can later be compensated for. This is the sense in which statistics is about explaining variance — *all* of the variance, including the parts of no direct interest.

The practical consequence is immediate: knowing the model, the data types and the design, the header row of the spreadsheet can be written before a single value is collected.

| Bloodpressure | Gender  | Concentration |          Time of day | Note |
|---------------|:-------:|--------------:|---------------------:|-----:|
| Numerical     | Nominal |     Numerical | Ordinal or numerical | Text |

That header row is not a formality. It is the model made concrete, and it is the first tidy-data decision of the study. Filled in row by row, **one experimental unit** at a time, the planned analysis is already half constructed.

## Where does the variation come from?

If statistics is about explaining variance, then good design begins by asking, from the model's point of view, *where the variance in the response actually originates*. It is useful to partition the total variation of the response into named sources:

$$SST = SSH + SSR + \underbrace{(SSE + SSM + SSU)}_{\textbf{residual}}$$

Each term is read as a physical source rather than an algebraic symbol:

- **SSH — the hypothesis.** Variation due to the conditions the hypothesis actually concerns. This is the signal to be detected.
- **SSE — the experimental unit.** Natural, irreducible variation between units: one rat is simply not another rat. This is legitimate biological noise.
- **SSR — repeated or longitudinal structure.** Variation arising from measuring the same unit more than once. This is the term that resampling has to respect on Day 7, when whole patients or plates, rather than single rows, become the unit that is left out.
- **SSM — measurement.** Variation and bias introduced by the act of measuring: instrument drift, calibration error, operator differences.
- **SSU — the unknown.** Variation from factors never identified — confounders, lurking covariates, the effect nobody considered.

The partition matters because the last three terms are dangerous in a way the first two are not. SSE is clean noise the model expects. But **SSM and SSU can violate the assumptions on which the analysis rests**: they can distort the residual distribution, destroy homoscedasticity, manufacture outliers or, worst of all, align with the treatment by accident and masquerade as signal. Much of experimental design is a set of tactics for keeping SSM and SSU out of the part of the variance that will later be attributed to the hypothesis.

## What must be considered before starting

Concretely, two families of variance and bias deserve explicit thought before the experiment begins.

*Variance and bias inherent to the system.* Chiefly: what **effect size** is expected? A number is required, and it may come from the literature, from previous experiments or — clearly labelled as such — from an educated guess. Without it the study cannot be sized.

*Variance and bias introduced by the experiment itself.* What noise does *conducting* the experiment add? Considerations include the distribution of the experimental random noise; systematic error from sensor drift or confounders such as weather; the variance within an experimentally defined block (which will become a random effect); and differences between laboratories or analysts performing the measurements. Separately, the sources of **bias** must be considered. The obvious sources are the researcher and the research question themselves — hoping for a particular result subtly nudges the countless small choices a study requires, from which animals to include to when to stop collecting data.

## The four levers: control, randomisation, replication, blocking

The aim of experimental design is to reduce, or explicitly account for, the impact of extraneous variables. Done well, it increases the power and precision of the eventual analysis at no cost — no extra data, only better-structured data. There are four classical levers, and the remainder of this chapter takes them in turn: **control, randomisation, replication and blocking.**

### Control

A control is a comparison built into the design so that a result can be interpreted. Different problems call for different kinds:

- **Negative control (the $H_0$ comparison).** The treatment stripped of its active ingredient — a placebo injection of the insulin solution *without* the insulin. Comparing a treatment against a negative control is the most direct possible test of the null hypothesis.
- **Positive control (the $H_A$ check).** A condition that is confidently expected to produce an effect, used to confirm that the setup can detect one at all — a deliberately high concentration that must register if the assay functions.
- **Initial-conditions control.** A baseline reading used to compensate for drift — recording a sensor's signal before the manipulation so that the slow wander of, for example, a pH electrode or its amplifier can be subtracted.

Each control targets a specific term in the variance partition. The negative control isolates SSH; the initial-conditions control attacks SSM.

### Randomisation

Randomisation is the tool for the most insidious term, SSU — the confounders, known and unknown. Its purpose is to ensure that whatever was not controlled does not systematically align with the treatment. Done correctly, it "averages out" the confounders, converting a potential bias into ordinary noise. Three distinct problems it defends against deserve names:

- **Systematic design artefacts.** A non-random offset built into the physical layout — a moisture gradient across a field, a temperature gradient across a 96-well plate, an edge effect.
- **Unconscious bias.** Non-random structure that enters without deliberate design, through the many small choices an experimenter makes.
- **Undesirable subjectivity.** The specific failure of humans asked to *be* random. Humans are extraordinarily poor at generating random sequences by hand, and the patterns they produce are predictable.

### A worked picture: the shaded field

Consider a field of 16 plots (or a plate of 16 wells) laid out in an orderly design, with treatments 1–4 assigned in neat columns. Suppose one edge of the field lies in shade for part of the day. Those plots receive fewer sun-hours and grow less — and because the layout was systematic, the shade falls disproportionately on treatments 1 and 3. The shade, an SSU effect, has become confounded with treatment. The analysis will report a "treatment effect" that is partly sunlight.

![A systematic layout: treatments assigned in neat columns. The grey area is shade, which falls disproportionately on treatments 1 and 3.](Figs/field.png){#fig-field width="70%"}

Randomising the assignment of treatments to plots breaks that alignment. After randomisation the shade is distributed across all four treatments; no single treatment carries its full weight. One treatment may still be somewhat over-represented in the shade by chance, but — and this is the essential point — **that imbalance shrinks as replicates are added.** Randomisation together with replication is what turns a confounder into harmless noise.

![The same field after randomising treatments to plots. The shade is now shared across all four treatments rather than confounded with two of them.](Figs/fieldR.png){#fig-field-random width="70%"}

### Unconscious bias

Unconscious bias is harder to detect precisely because it appears reasonable at the time. Each of the following examples sounds acceptable until examined twice:

- Testing food preference "in humans" using a taste panel of women over 55.
- Studying adrenaline's effect on skeletal muscle using only young mice.
- Assigning "the first ten larvae out of the box" to treatment 1 and the next ten to treatment 2 — as if the order in which they are caught carried no information (it does: the slow, the sick and the bold are not caught at random).

Beyond the biology, other pressures bias designs in systematic directions: cost, ethics and time all push towards the convenient choice. There is no statistical remedy for these. The only defence is sustained criticism of one's own reasoning and alertness to the forms these biases take.

### A subtle case: spatial confounders

Suppose 10 trees must be selected "at random" from a forest to test a pest-control chemical. A tempting method is to close one's eyes, place a finger on ten points of the map, and take the nearest tree to each.

This is not a random sample. Trees are not uniformly spaced. Where trees cluster densely, each individual tree captures a small catchment of "nearest" points; where trees are sparse — near a clearing or a pond — a lone tree captures a large catchment and is far more likely to be chosen. The "random" points are uniform over *space*, but the selection probability is therefore biased towards *isolated* trees, which may differ systematically (more light, less competition) from trees within the stand. The spatial structure has become a confounder.

The two panels below make the trap visible. The first shows the "random" points dropped on the map; the second overlays where trees actually grow (the shaded clusters).





::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Code for plot below"}
set.seed(234)
x <- runif(50, 0, 10)
y <- runif(50, 0, 10)

op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(3, 3, 3, 1))

plot(x, y, col = "blue", pch = 19, main = "Points dropped 'at random'",
     xlab = "", ylab = "")

plot(x, y, type = "n", main = "...but trees are not uniform",
     xlab = "", ylab = "")
polygon(c(0, 0.5, 2, 3, 4), c(10, 8.2, 8, 9.3, 10), col = "lightblue", lwd = 1)
polygon(c(5.4, 6.0, 6.1, 5.8), c(3, 3.3, 4, 3.8), col = "lightblue", lwd = 1)
points(x, y, pch = 19, col = "blue")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](02-design_files/figure-html/spatial-confounder-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768}
:::

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Code for plot below"}
par(op)
```
:::





In the right-hand panel, a point landing near an isolated tree in the sparse regions selects that lone tree, while a point landing in a dense cluster is shared among many candidates; the isolated trees are therefore systematically over-selected.

The remedy is to remove space from the selection entirely: every tree is labelled and the labels are drawn at random, by computer or from an urn. Any spatial or temporal relationship among the trees is then averaged out by construction, rather than introduced by the geometry of "nearest".

### Replication — and the experimental unit

Before replicates can be counted, it must be established *what* is being replicated. This is the single most misunderstood idea in the lecture, and misunderstanding it is the classic route to an incorrect analysis, so it is stated carefully.

> The **experimental unit** is the smallest division of the experimental material such that any two units could receive different independent treatments.

Equivalently: all sample units (individual measurements) *within* an experimental unit necessarily receive the same treatment. If six measurements share a confinement — a plot, a cage, a subject — and that confinement is what receives the treatment, then the confinement, not the individual measurement, is the experimental unit. The number of *independent* replicates is the number of experimental units, and it is that number — not the number of measurements — from which the degrees of freedom for the treatment are built.

The abstraction is slippery, and four cases are worked through. In each, two questions should be posed before reading on: *what is the experimental unit, and how many independent replicates are there?*

![Case 1: each rat is individually injected with placebo (A) or vitamin C (B).](Figs/rats.png){#fig-rats1 width="70%"}

**Case 1 — individually injected rats.** Six rats, each *individually injected* with either a placebo or vitamin C, three per group. Each animal receives its own treatment, with all the particularities of its own injection, independently of the others. The **rat is the experimental unit**, and there are six independent replicates — three per treatment.

![Case 2: rats share a box, and each box receives one diet — water or water with vitamin C.](Figs/rats2.png){#fig-rats2 width="80%"}

**Case 2 — rats sharing a cage diet.** The vitamin C is now delivered through the drinking water, and rats are housed two to a box, each box on one diet. The two rats in a box share the same water, the same local temperature, and everything else particular to that box, but also competition for the water and possible diseases they will share; their measurements are not independent. The **box is the experimental unit.** With, say, two boxes per treatment there are four independent replicates, not eight, regardless of how many rats each box contains.

![Case 3: two rat strains with known different baseline adrenaline levels.](Figs/rats3.png){#fig-rats3 width="80%"}

**Case 3 — nested strains.** The hypothesis is that aggression relates to resting blood adrenaline, tested using two rat strains known to differ in baseline adrenaline. Here the "adrenaline treatment" is not applied to rats; it is a property of the *strain*. The treatment is **nested in strain**, and the strain is the experimental unit. With only two strains there are effectively two experimental units for the contrast, however many rats each contains — a genuinely weak design for the question, and one worth recognising as such *before* it is run.

![Case 4: each rat's liver is chopped into six pieces for fat-content analysis.](Figs/rats4.png){#fig-rats4 width="70%"}

**Case 4 — pieces of one liver.** Rats A–C receive a standard vitamin C diet, D–F a high one; each rat's liver is then divided into six pieces for fat-content analysis. It is tempting to claim 36 replicates. But the six pieces of one liver are genetically and historically the same animal; if that rat had liver disease, all six pieces carry it. The pieces are **nested in rat**; the **rat is the experimental unit**, giving three replicates per diet. Analysing the 36 pieces as if independent is *pseudoreplication*, and it makes the result appear far more certain than it is.

The thread through all four cases is the one connecting this lecture to the next. Whenever measurements share a confinement, a subject or a lineage, they are **correlated**, and treating them as independent inflates the effective sample size and shrinks the standard errors illegitimately. Recognising these dependencies now is what allows them to be respected later: on Day 7, boxes, strains and rats become the units that are resampled and held out together.

### Blocking

Blocking is the fourth lever, and the constructive counterpart to randomisation. Where randomisation *averages out* a nuisance factor, blocking *accounts for it explicitly.* The two are not rivals; they are the two available responses to structure that was not intended, and the choice between them turns on one question: *is the nuisance known to be present?* If not, randomise. If so, block.

It is instructive to see all three responses to the same problem side by side, because they are literally the same field drawn three ways. In the **systematic** layout of the shaded field, treatments sat in neat columns and the shade fell squarely on treatments 1 and 3: the confounder was perfectly aligned with the treatment, and the analysis had no way to distinguish sunlight from effect. **Randomising** the assignment broke that alignment: the shade was scattered across all four treatments, and with sufficient replicates its influence averaged towards zero. But randomisation pays for that with variance — the shade remains *in* the residual, inflating $\sigma$ and costing power.

Blocking does something more refined. If the shade is *known* to run across the field, the field is divided into blocks chosen to be internally homogeneous with respect to it — a shaded half and a sunny half — and **every treatment appears once in every block**, in randomised order within each. The sun-hour difference now lives entirely *between* the blocks, where the analysis can estimate it and set it aside. It never touches the treatment comparison, because every treatment experienced the shade equally. This is a randomised complete block design: the same field, divided along the gradient it was fighting.





::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Plot generating code"}
cols <- c(T1 = "#7F77DD", T2 = "#D85A30", T3 = "#1D9E75", T4 = "#BA7517")

plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 5.2), axes = FALSE,
     xlab = "", ylab = "",
     main = "Randomised complete block: the same field, split along the shade")

# shade gradient: darker (less sun) on the left, fading to the right
ng <- 100
for (i in 1:ng) {
  rect((i - 1) * 10 / ng, 0.4, i * 10 / ng, 4.4,
       col = rgb(0.37, 0.37, 0.35, 0.40 * (1 - (i - 1) / ng)), border = NA)
}
text(0.4, 4.8, "Less sun", adj = 0, cex = 0.9)
text(9.6, 4.8, "More sun", adj = 1, cex = 0.9)

# the two blocks
rect(0.2, 0.5, 4.8, 4.3, border = "grey40", lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)
rect(5.2, 0.5, 9.8, 4.3, border = "grey40", lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)
text(2.5, 4.05, "Block 1 (shaded)", font = 2, cex = 0.95)
text(7.5, 4.05, "Block 2 (sunny)",  font = 2, cex = 0.95)

# helper: draw one plot cell
cell <- function(x, y, tr) {
  rect(x, y, x + 2, y + 1.4, col = cols[tr], border = "white", lwd = 2)
  text(x + 1, y + 0.7, tr, col = "white", font = 2, cex = 1.3)
}

# each block holds all four treatments, order randomised within the block
cell(0.5, 2.3, "T3"); cell(2.7, 2.3, "T1")
cell(0.5, 0.7, "T4"); cell(2.7, 0.7, "T2")
cell(5.5, 2.3, "T2"); cell(7.7, 2.3, "T4")
cell(5.5, 0.7, "T1"); cell(7.7, 0.7, "T3")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](02-design_files/figure-html/blocking-field-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768}
:::
:::





The figure shows both blocks containing all four treatments, with the shade gradient running between rather than within blocks. The payoff is real and quantifiable: the between-block variation that randomisation left in the residual is now removed from it, $\sigma$ shrinks, and — by the power heuristic introduced below — power rises at no cost in sample size. The same logic applies to any nuisance that can be named in advance: the day of the week, the technician, the shelf in the incubator, the litter a mouse came from. What can be identified is blocked; what cannot is randomised against. A further connection runs beneath this: a block is a source of shared structure among its units, just like the box and the rat before it. In bioinformatics the most familiar block is the sequencing or hybridisation **batch**, and a batch that is confounded with the biological groups cannot be repaired afterwards.

### Integration: the four levers as one strategy

The four levers address the variance partition from different directions. Control fixes the comparison so that SSH can be isolated and SSM corrected; randomisation converts unknown SSU from bias into noise; replication at the level of the experimental unit determines how many independent observations of that noise exist; and blocking removes known nuisance variation from the residual altogether. All four are decided before any data are collected, and all four determine the denominator — the residual variance and its degrees of freedom — against which the treatment effect will eventually be judged. The next section makes that judgement quantitative.

## Type I and type II error, and power

The vocabulary is now available to make "large enough" precise. Every hypothesis test can be wrong in two distinct ways, and it is essential to keep them separate.

A **type I error** is rejecting a true null — declaring an effect that is not present. Its probability is $\alpha$, the significance level chosen by the analyst:

$$P(\text{reject } H_0 \mid H_0 \text{ true}) = \alpha$$

A **type II error** is failing to reject a false null — missing an effect that is real. Its probability is $\beta$:

$$P(\text{not reject } H_0 \mid H_0 \text{ false}) = \beta$$

The **power** of a test is the complement of $\beta$ — the probability of detecting an effect that is genuinely present:

$$\text{Power} = P(\text{reject } H_0 \mid H_0 \text{ false}) = 1 - \beta$$

The quantity $\alpha$ is the accepted risk of a false alarm; power is the probability of detecting a real effect. Good design fixes the first and maximises the second.

### What drives power

The exact formula is not needed to build correct intuition. A heuristic captures the direction of every lever:

$$\text{Power} \;\propto\; \frac{\text{effect size} \times \alpha \times \sqrt{n}}{\sigma}$$

The expression may be read as a set of dials. Three quantities in the numerator *raise* power: a larger true **effect size**, a more permissive $\alpha$, and a larger **sample size** (through $\sqrt{n}$ — returns diminish, since quadrupling $n$ only doubles this term). One quantity in the denominator *lowers* power: the residual standard deviation $\sigma$, the noise. This is why everything earlier in the chapter mattered — control, blocking and clean measurement all attack $\sigma$, and every reduction in $\sigma$ purchases power without a single additional sample.

### Power as overlapping curves

The most useful mental image is two sampling distributions of the mean — one under $H_0$, one under $H_A$ — placed side by side on the same axis. The critical values (set by $\alpha$) mark the cut-offs beyond which $H_0$ is rejected. The type I error is the tail of the *null* curve that extends past the critical value; the type II error, $\beta$, is the portion of the *alternative* curve that falls *short* of it, in the non-rejection region. Power is the remainder of the alternative curve — the part that clears the cut-off.

The effect of each dial on the picture follows directly. Increasing the effect size slides the two curves apart; less of the alternative curve overlaps the non-rejection region, so $\beta$ shrinks and power grows. Decreasing $\sigma$ narrows both curves; again the overlap falls. Increasing $n$ tightens the sampling distributions of the mean (their spread is $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$), pulling the curves apart in standardised terms. Every route to more power is, in this picture, a route to *less overlap* between the null and alternative distributions.





::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Code plot below"}
Length_M <- seq(8, 26, 0.01)
Density  <- dnorm(Length_M, 18, 2)   # distribution under H0 (mean 18)
Density2 <- dnorm(Length_M, 15, 2)   # distribution under HA (mean 15)

# critical value from the H0 curve
Critm <- 18 - 2 * 2.048

plot(Density2 ~ Length_M, type = "l", col = "red", lwd = 3,
     ylab = "Density", xlab = "Sample mean",
     main = "Two distributions of the mean: power as non-overlap")

# beta: the part of the HA curve in the non-rejection region (right of critical value)
cord.x <- c(Critm, seq(Critm, 25, 0.01), 25)
cord.y <- c(0, dnorm(seq(Critm, 25, 0.01), 15, 2), 0)
polygon(cord.x, cord.y, col = "red")

# power: the part of the HA curve past the critical value (left tail here)
cord.x <- c(8, seq(8, Critm, 0.01), Critm)
cord.y <- c(0, dnorm(seq(8, Critm, 0.01), 15, 2), 0)
polygon(cord.x, cord.y, col = "darkgreen")

arrows(Critm, 0.06, Critm, 0.02, lwd = 3)
text(Critm, 0.07, "critical value")
text(16, 0.05, expression(beta), cex = 3)

lines(Density ~ Length_M, col = "blue", lwd = 3)  # H0 for reference
abline(0, 0); segments(15, 0, 15, dnorm(15, 15, 2), lty = 2)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](02-design_files/figure-html/overlap-curves-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768}
:::
:::





The blue curve is **the sampling distribution of the mean** under $H_0$ and the red curve that under $H_A$. The red shaded area to the right of the critical value is $\beta$: the alternative is true, yet the sample mean falls in the non-rejection region. The green area to the left is the power. Everything else in this section is that picture, moved by one dial at a time.

### Computing power in R

R reduces all of this to a one-line calculation for the two-sample $t$-test, and the same function answers two different questions depending on which argument is left unspecified.

**Post-hoc: the study has been run — what power did it have?** With $n$ and the effect size fixed, the power is requested. This is a check after the fact, and its legitimate use is to inform the next study, not to excuse a null result.





::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
power.t.test(n = 15, delta = 1, sd = 2, sig.level = 0.05,
             alternative = "two.sided")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> 
#>      Two-sample t test power calculation 
#> 
#>               n = 15
#>           delta = 1
#>              sd = 2
#>       sig.level = 0.05
#>           power = 0.2619313
#>     alternative = two.sided
#> 
#> NOTE: n is number in *each* group
```


:::
:::





With 15 observations per group, a true difference of 1 and a standard deviation of 2, the power is approximately 0.26: a real effect of this size would be detected in roughly one study in four. A null result from such a study is uninformative.

**A priori: the study is being planned — how many replicates are needed?** The desired power (0.8 is the usual minimum), the effect size and $\sigma$ are fixed, and $n$ is solved for. This is the calculation that should precede the experiment, and it is the whole point of Fisher's warning.





::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
power.t.test(power = 0.8, delta = 1, sd = 2, sig.level = 0.05,
             alternative = "two.sided")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> 
#>      Two-sample t test power calculation 
#> 
#>               n = 63.76576
#>           delta = 1
#>              sd = 2
#>       sig.level = 0.05
#>           power = 0.8
#>     alternative = two.sided
#> 
#> NOTE: n is number in *each* group
```


:::
:::





The required sample size is approximately 64 per group — more than four times the 15 used in the post-hoc example. The difference between the two calculations is the cost of the noise: with $\sigma$ twice the effect size, many observations are needed to separate signal from residual variation.

The procedure for using power well is therefore a fixed sequence of decisions:

1.  Fix the type I risk to be accepted — set $\alpha$ (e.g. 0.05).
2.  Decide the minimum power required — e.g. 0.8.
3.  Decide the smallest **biologically significant** effect size — the smallest effect that would actually matter, not the smallest one detectable.
4.  Obtain a defensible estimate of $\sigma$ — from the literature, a similar experiment, or a pilot study.

With those four numbers, an a priori analysis returns the required $n$. After the study, a post-hoc analysis reports the power that was actually attained.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Where the number 64 comes from"}
The number 64 is not magic, and a short derivation shows where it comes from. Take two groups of $n$ observations with a true difference $\delta$ and a known standard deviation $\sigma$. The difference of the two sample means is normally distributed,

$$\bar x_1 - \bar x_2 \sim N\!\left(\delta,\ \frac{2\sigma^2}{n}\right),$$

so the test statistic $z = (\bar x_1 - \bar x_2)\big/\big(\sigma\sqrt{2/n}\big)$ is standard normal under $H_0$ and is shifted by $\delta\big/\big(\sigma\sqrt{2/n}\big)$ under $H_A$. The null hypothesis is rejected when $|z| > z_{1-\alpha/2}$. Ignoring the negligible chance of rejecting in the wrong direction,

$$\text{Power} \approx P\!\left(Z > z_{1-\alpha/2} - \frac{\delta}{\sigma\sqrt{2/n}}\right).$$

Requiring this to equal $1 - \beta$ means that the shift must be $z_{1-\alpha/2} + z_{1-\beta}$, and solving for $n$ gives

$$n = \frac{2\,(z_{1-\alpha/2} + z_{1-\beta})^2\,\sigma^2}{\delta^2} \quad\text{per group.}$$





::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
delta <- 1; sigma <- 2
c(normal_formula = 2 * (qnorm(0.975) + qnorm(0.80))^2 * sigma^2 / delta^2,
  power.t.test   = power.t.test(power = 0.8, delta = delta, sd = sigma)$n)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> normal_formula   power.t.test 
#>       62.79104       63.76576
```


:::
:::





The formula gives 62.8, and `power.t.test` gives one more, because it uses the $t$ distribution: $\sigma$ has to be estimated, which costs a little power. The formula also makes the heuristic of the previous section exact. Power depends on the data only through $\delta\sqrt{n}/\sigma$. Halving the effect size, or doubling the noise, therefore *quadruples* the number of units required.
:::

### Power without a formula: simulation

`power.t.test` has a formula behind it, but there is a more transparent way to determine power that generalises to any design, however complex — *simulate the whole experiment many times and count how often it succeeds.* This is worth doing at least once explicitly, because it demystifies power completely and because the practicals rely on exactly this skill.

A single simulated experiment comes first. Fifteen "males" are drawn from a normal distribution with mean length 18 and SD 2, fifteen "females" with mean 17 and SD 2, and one $t$-test is run.





::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(1)
Males   <- rnorm(15, mean = 18, sd = 2)
Females <- rnorm(15, mean = 17, sd = 2)
t.test(Males, Females)$p.value
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 0.1295293
```


:::
:::





That single p-value is one draw from a random process; it is not, on its own, informative about power. Power is a long-run frequency, so the whole experiment is repeated 10,000 times and the fraction of runs in which the effect was correctly detected ($p < 0.05$) is recorded. That fraction *is* the power.





::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pval <- numeric(10000)
for (i in 1:10000) {
  A <- rnorm(20, 18, 2)   # true difference is 1, SD is 2
  B <- rnorm(20, 17, 2)
  pval[i] <- t.test(A, B)$p.value
}
sum(pval < 0.05) / 10000   # estimated power at n = 20
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 0.3409
```


:::
:::





The simulated power at $n = 20$ per group is approximately 0.34, consistent with the analytic value from `power.t.test` for the same parameters. The logic is entirely explicit: the effect is *known* to be real because it was built in, so every failure to reject is a genuine type II error, and their frequency is $\beta$. Raising $n$ from 20 to 40 and re-running shows the power climb — the same lesson as the heuristic formula, obtained by direct bookkeeping rather than by trusting an equation.

### The power curve

Sweeping $n$ across a range and plotting the resulting power traces a **power curve**, the single most useful object for planning. Reading off where the curve crosses 0.8 gives the required sample size. The analytic version is a smooth line; the simulated version is the same curve, scattered by Monte Carlo noise. Their agreement is the point: the formula and the simulation compute the same quantity in two different ways.





::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
NN    <- 3:200
Power <- power.t.test(n = NN, delta = 1, sd = 2, sig.level = 0.05,
                      type = "two.sample", alternative = "two.sided")$power
plot(Power ~ NN, type = "l", lwd = 3, ylim = c(0, 1),
     main = "Power curve for the two-sample t-test",
     xlab = "n per group", ylab = "Power")
segments(-5, 0.8, 64, 0.8, lty = 2)
arrows(64, 0.8, 64, 0.05, lty = 2)
text(64, 0.02, "n = 64")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](02-design_files/figure-html/power-curve-1.png){fig-align='center' width=768}
:::
:::





The dashed guides mark the crossing: approximately 64 per group to reach a power of 0.8 for this effect size and noise level, in agreement with the a priori calculation above. Changing the effect size or $\sigma$ shifts the entire curve — which is, once again, the message of the whole chapter. Power is not a property of the test alone; it is a property of the *design*.

### Integration: power as the summary of design

The three computations of this section — the analytic post-hoc and a priori calls, the simulation, and the power curve — are three views of one quantity. Each shows that power is determined jointly by the effect size, the residual standard deviation, the significance level and the sample size, and that the sample size in question is the number of experimental units. The design decisions of the first half of the chapter enter through $\sigma$ and $n$: blocking and control reduce $\sigma$, correct identification of the experimental unit determines the true $n$, and randomisation ensures that what remains in $\sigma$ is noise rather than bias. A power calculation performed before the experiment is therefore the point at which every earlier design decision is tested against the effect the study aims to detect.

## When the data come first {#sec-data-first}

Everything so far assumed that the hypothesis was fixed before the data existed. From Day 4 onwards that is rarely the case. PCA and clustering search the data for structure; classifiers search them for whatever separates the labels. Experimental design does not become irrelevant there. Some of its ideas carry over unchanged, some change their meaning, and one new requirement appears: an honest check on independent data has to be planned before the study starts.

### A pattern found in the data will be confirmed by the same data

Suppose 100 patients are measured on a panel of 50 genes, and the patients are clustered into two groups. A natural next step is to ask which genes differ between the two groups, with a *t*-test per gene. The tests will find differences, even if the patients were all the same: the clustering algorithm chose the split that makes the groups as different as possible, and the tests then ask whether the groups are different. The question has been answered before it was asked. This is called **circular analysis** or **double dipping** [@Kriegeskorte2009], and it is one of the most common errors in genomics.

The same trap exists for prediction. If the genes that best separate tumour from normal are selected using *all* samples, and a classifier built on those genes is then evaluated on part of the same samples, the evaluation is no longer independent of the selection. Accuracies of 90% are then easily obtained from pure noise [@Ambroise2002]. Exercises 2.1 and 2.2 below let you produce both effects yourself.

::: column-margin
**DEF** — **Double dipping**: using the same data first to choose a hypothesis (a split, a set of genes, a model) and then to test or evaluate it.
:::

The remedy is a design decision, not an analysis trick: **split the data, or the study, before looking.**

- Set aside a **validation set** (or test set) at random, and do not touch it until every choice has been made on the other part, the **discovery set** (or training set).
- Better still, plan an **independent replication cohort**: other patients, another hospital, another time. Genome-wide association studies have long required this, which is one reason why their findings replicate far better than those of the earlier candidate-gene studies, many of which did not replicate at all.
- Decide the split in advance, and size *both* parts. A validation set of ten samples cannot confirm anything.

::: column-margin
**↪** Day 7 develops this into cross-validation, where every sample takes a turn in the validation set, and into nested cross-validation, where every data-driven choice is kept inside the loop.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise 2.1 — Clusters from nothing"}
Simulate a study in which there is nothing to find: 100 patients, measured on a panel of 50 genes, all values independent standard normal.





::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(2026)
n <- 100; p <- 50
X <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), nrow = n, ncol = p)   # patients in rows, genes in columns
```
:::





a. Cluster the patients into two groups with `kmeans(X, centers = 2, nstart = 20)`. How large are the groups?
b. Test every gene for a difference between the two clusters with a *t*-test. How many genes have $p < 0.05$, and how many would you expect if there were no structure? How many survive a false-discovery-rate correction, `p.adjust(p_values, method = "BH")`?
c. Explain the result of (b) in one or two sentences.
d. Now do it honestly. Before clustering, split the patients at random into a discovery half and a validation half. Cluster each half separately. Then assign every validation patient to the *nearest discovery centre* and compare this assignment with the clustering of the validation half itself. Use the helper functions below. Repeat for a few different random splits.





::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# for every row of Xnew: the number of the nearest centre
nearest <- function(Xnew, centers)
  apply(Xnew, 1, function(x) which.min(colSums((t(centers) - x)^2)))
# fraction of patients on which two partitions agree (labels are arbitrary)
agree <- function(a, b) max(mean(a == b), mean(a != b))
```
:::





e. Give the patients a real subtype: add 1 to genes 1 to 10 for patients 51 to 100. Repeat (d). How does the agreement compare with that for pure noise?
f. You are planning a study to discover subtypes in 100 patients. Which decisions about discovery and validation should be written down before the samples are collected, and what does the split cost?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hints"}
For (b), loop over the columns: `sapply(1:p, function(j) t.test(X[cl == 1, j], X[cl == 2, j])$p.value)`. For (d), `disc <- sample(n, n / 2)` and `val <- setdiff(1:n, disc)` give the two halves; the centres of a clustering are in `km$centers`. An agreement of 0.5 means that the two partitions have nothing to do with each other; 1 means they are identical.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(2026)
n <- 100; p <- 50
X  <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), nrow = n, ncol = p)

# (a) and (b): cluster, then test the clusters
cl <- kmeans(X, centers = 2, nstart = 20)$cluster
p_values <- sapply(1:p, function(j) t.test(X[cl == 1, j], X[cl == 2, j])$p.value)
c(cluster_sizes = table(cl), p_below_0.05 = sum(p_values < 0.05),
  expected = 0.05 * p, after_BH = sum(p.adjust(p_values, method = "BH") < 0.05))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> cluster_sizes.1 cluster_sizes.2    p_below_0.05        expected        after_BH 
#>            50.0            50.0            18.0             2.5            10.0
```


:::
:::





(c) There is no structure in these data, yet about a third of the genes "differ" between the clusters, and several survive the false-discovery-rate correction. The clustering chose the split that separates the patients as much as possible along some combination of genes; the *t*-tests then confirm that this split separates the patients. The *p*-values assume that the groups were defined independently of the data, and they were not.





::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
nearest <- function(Xnew, centers)
  apply(Xnew, 1, function(x) which.min(colSums((t(centers) - x)^2)))
agree <- function(a, b) max(mean(a == b), mean(a != b))

replicate_split <- function(X, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  disc <- sample(nrow(X), nrow(X) / 2); val <- setdiff(seq_len(nrow(X)), disc)
  km_disc <- kmeans(X[disc, ], centers = 2, nstart = 20)
  km_val  <- kmeans(X[val, ],  centers = 2, nstart = 20)
  agree(nearest(X[val, ], km_disc$centers), km_val$cluster)
}

Y <- X
Y[51:100, 1:10] <- Y[51:100, 1:10] + 1          # (e) a real subtype

rbind(pure_noise   = sapply(1:8, function(s) replicate_split(X, s)),
      real_subtype = sapply(1:8, function(s) replicate_split(Y, s)))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>              [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5] [,6] [,7] [,8]
#> pure_noise   0.54 0.62 0.58 0.52 0.50 0.54 0.60 0.64
#> real_subtype 0.90 0.74 0.84 0.82 0.78 0.88 0.86 0.86
```


:::
:::





(d, e) For pure noise the agreement stays close to 0.5: the discovery clustering found a split, but a different split appears in new patients. With a real subtype the agreement is clearly higher, because the same structure is present in both halves. It is not perfect, because 50 patients are not many for finding a difference spread over 10 of 50 genes.

(f) Before collecting samples: how the patients will be divided (random, and stratified by hospital or batch if these exist), the size of each part, that the validation part will not be looked at until the discovery analysis is finished, and what counts as a successful replication. The cost is that each analysis has only half the patients, so a weaker structure may be missed in discovery, as the imperfect agreement in (e) shows. Sizing the study must take both halves into account, or plan an independent cohort.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise 2.2 — Selecting genes before testing a classifier"}
Simulate 40 samples on 1,000 genes of pure noise, and give them labels: 20 "tumour" and 20 "normal". The labels carry no information. A **nearest-centroid classifier** assigns a new sample to the class whose mean profile is closest; it is given below, together with a fast *t*-test for every column of a matrix.





::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
nearest_centroid_accuracy <- function(X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test) {
  m1 <- colMeans(X_train[y_train == 1, , drop = FALSE])
  m2 <- colMeans(X_train[y_train == 2, , drop = FALSE])
  d1 <- rowSums(sweep(X_test, 2, m1)^2)
  d2 <- rowSums(sweep(X_test, 2, m2)^2)
  mean(ifelse(d1 < d2, 1, 2) == y_test)
}
# two-sample t-test for every column of X at once
column_t_pvalues <- function(X, y) {
  a <- X[y == 1, , drop = FALSE]; b <- X[y == 2, , drop = FALSE]
  ss_a <- colSums(sweep(a, 2, colMeans(a))^2)
  ss_b <- colSums(sweep(b, 2, colMeans(b))^2)
  s2 <- (ss_a + ss_b) / (nrow(a) + nrow(b) - 2)
  t <- (colMeans(a) - colMeans(b)) / sqrt(s2 * (1 / nrow(a) + 1 / nrow(b)))
  2 * pt(-abs(t), nrow(a) + nrow(b) - 2)
}
```
:::





a. Using all 40 samples, select the 20 genes with the smallest *p*-values. Then split the samples into a training half and a test half (10 of each class in each half), build the classifier on the training half with the selected genes, and compute its accuracy on the test half.
b. Repeat, but now select the 20 genes using the training half only.
c. Repeat (a) and (b) 100 times with new data, and report the average accuracy of each.
d. Which of the two numbers would you expect to see in a paper, and why is this a problem of design rather than of analysis?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
one_study <- function() {
  X <- matrix(rnorm(40 * 1000), nrow = 40)
  y <- rep(1:2, each = 20)
  train <- c(sample(1:20, 10), sample(21:40, 10)); test <- setdiff(1:40, train)
  genes_all   <- order(column_t_pvalues(X, y))[1:20]                     # (a)
  genes_train <- order(column_t_pvalues(X[train, ], y[train]))[1:20]     # (b)
  acc_all   <- nearest_centroid_accuracy(X[train, genes_all], y[train],
                                         X[test, genes_all], y[test])
  acc_train <- nearest_centroid_accuracy(X[train, genes_train], y[train],
                                         X[test, genes_train], y[test])
  c(selected_on_all_samples = acc_all, selected_on_training_only = acc_train)
}
set.seed(1)
rowMeans(replicate(100, one_study()))                                     # (c)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>   selected_on_all_samples selected_on_training_only 
#>                    0.9385                    0.5065
```


:::
:::





(d) Selecting on all samples gives an accuracy above 90% for labels that carry no information; selecting on the training half gives the honest 50%. The first number is the one that looks publishable, and versions of it have been published [@Ambroise2002]. The test samples took part in choosing the genes, so they were no longer independent of the model. No later analysis can repair this: the remedy is to lock the test set away *before* the first data-driven decision, which is a matter of how the study is organised.
:::

### Collect the variation, and record it

A confirmatory design keeps nuisance variation small, because every bit of it costs power. Exploration needs almost the opposite. Subtypes can only be discovered in a sample that contains them, so the sample should span the variation that might matter: disease stages, ages, both sexes, several hospitals. A homogeneous sample is efficient for a test but blind for discovery.

The price is that this variation must be **recorded**. In exploration nobody knows in advance which variable will turn out to explain a cluster or a principal component, so every piece of metadata should be kept: age, sex, tissue, RNA quality, date of extraction, operator, sequencing run, position on the plate. A cluster that coincides with the extraction date is a finding about the laboratory, not about the disease, and it can only be recognised as such if the date was written down.

::: column-margin
**KEY** — Confirmatory design minimises nuisance variation. Exploratory design samples the variation broadly and records its sources.
:::

### Batches: the four levers still apply

The levers of this chapter return almost unchanged in the laboratory part of a data-driven study, and they matter even more, because an exploratory method will find *any* strong source of variation, including the technical ones [@Leek2010]. Consider 24 samples, 12 tumour and 12 normal, sequenced in two runs of 12. Suppose there is no biological difference at all, but the second run reads 100 of the 500 genes slightly higher. The figure compares two ways of filling the runs.





::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Code for the figure"}
set.seed(42)
n <- 24; p <- 500
group    <- rep(c("tumour", "normal"), each = 12)
run_conf <- ifelse(group == "tumour", "run 1", "run 2")          # confounded design
run_bal  <- rep(rep(c("run 1", "run 2"), each = 6), 2)           # balanced design
simulate <- function(run) {
  X <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p)
  X[run == "run 2", 1:100] <- X[run == "run 2", 1:100] + 1       # technical effect only
  X
}
X_conf <- simulate(run_conf); X_bal <- simulate(run_bal)

draw <- function(X, run, main) {
  pc <- prcomp(X)$x
  plot(pc[, 1], pc[, 2], pch = ifelse(run == "run 1", 19, 17), cex = 1.4,
       col = ifelse(group == "tumour", "#D35400", "#1F4E79"), las = 1,
       xlab = "first principal component", ylab = "second principal component", main = main)
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2.5, 1))
draw(X_conf, run_conf, "confounded: group = run")
legend("top", bty = "n", cex = 0.8, ncol = 2, pch = c(19, 19, 19, 17),
       col = c("#D35400", "#1F4E79", "grey40", "grey40"),
       legend = c("tumour", "normal", "run 1", "run 2"))
draw(X_bal, run_bal, "balanced: both groups in each run")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![The same technical batch effect, and no biological difference, in two designs. The samples are drawn by principal component analysis (Day 4), which places them along the directions in which they differ most. Left: all tumours were sequenced in run 1 and all normals in run 2. The two groups separate perfectly, and nothing in the data can show that this is the run. Right: each run contains six tumours and six normals. The first component now separates the runs, and within each run tumours and normals are mixed: there is no biological signal, and the run effect can be estimated and removed.](02-design_files/figure-html/fig-batch-1.png){#fig-batch width=816}
:::
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# genes declared "differentially expressed" at a false discovery rate of 5%
p_conf <- apply(X_conf, 2, function(g) t.test(g ~ group)$p.value)
p_bal  <- apply(X_bal,  2, function(g) anova(lm(g ~ run_bal + group))["group", "Pr(>F)"])
c(confounded = sum(p.adjust(p_conf, "BH") < 0.05),
  balanced_with_run_in_model = sum(p.adjust(p_bal, "BH") < 0.05))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>                 confounded balanced_with_run_in_model 
#>                         22                          0
```


:::
:::





In the confounded design, the analysis reports a clean separation and a list of "differentially expressed" genes, none of which is real. In the balanced design, the run is a block: it can be put in the model, and the false discoveries disappear. The levers translate directly:

- **Blocking and randomisation** → spread the biological groups evenly over runs, plates, extraction days and technicians, and randomise the positions within each.
- **Control** → include technical replicates, reference samples or pooled quality-control samples in every run; they measure the variation added by the measurement itself (SSM).
- **The experimental unit** → know which samples come from the same patient, mouse or culture. Several biopsies per patient form clusters that are simply patients, and on Day 7 they decide how the data may be split.

::: column-margin
**⚠** A batch that is confounded with the biological groups cannot be corrected afterwards. Batch-correction methods need both groups present in every batch.
:::

::: {.callout-caution title="Check yourself"}
A colleague has 48 RNA samples, 24 from responders and 24 from non-responders, and a sequencer that takes 16 samples per run. She proposes to sequence the responders first, because their samples arrived first. What would you advise, and what should be recorded?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Use three runs, each with 8 responders and 8 non-responders, with the positions within each run randomised. Sequencing the responders first would confound response with run, and possibly with storage time as well. Record the run, the position, the extraction date and the arrival date for every sample, so that any of these can be checked or put in the model later.
:::
:::

### How many samples, when there is no hypothesis to power?

There is no effect size to plug into `power.t.test` when the question is "are there subtypes?". Sample size still matters, and it can still be reasoned about.

- **Rare groups.** A subtype that makes up 5% of patients can only be discovered if enough of its members are in the sample. To have a 90% chance of including at least ten of them requires almost 300 patients (see below).
- **Stable structure.** A principal component or a cluster should be a property of the population, not of this sample. Exercise 2.1 showed that 50 patients recovered a real subtype only imperfectly. For PCA there is even a sharp limit, known from random-matrix theory: with many more genes than samples, a direction with a modest amount of extra variance cannot be distinguished from noise at all, however carefully it is measured.
- **The precision of an error rate.** An accuracy measured on $n$ test samples has a standard error of about $\sqrt{a(1-a)/n}$. With 50 test samples and an accuracy of 80%, that is almost six percentage points, more than many of the "improvements" reported between classifiers.





::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# (1) patients needed for a 90% chance of at least 10 members of a 5% subtype
n_try <- 50:600
min(n_try[1 - pbinom(9, n_try, 0.05) >= 0.9])
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 282
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# (3) standard error of an 80% accuracy, and the test size for a 95% interval of +/- 5%
c(se_50_test_samples = sqrt(0.8 * 0.2 / 50),
  n_for_plus_minus_5 = ceiling(0.8 * 0.2 * (1.96 / 0.05)^2))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> se_50_test_samples n_for_plus_minus_5 
#>         0.05656854       246.00000000
```


:::
:::





Where no formula applies, a pilot study and a simulation of the planned analysis, in the style of the power simulation above, answer the same question.

### Confirming what was found: the winner's curse

Exploration ends with a hypothesis, and testing it is a confirmatory study like any other, with randomisation and a power calculation. There is one trap. The effect size for the power calculation is naturally taken from the discovery data, and that estimate is too large. The genes, clusters or predictors that were carried forward were chosen *because* they looked strongest, and looking strongest is partly luck. This is the **winner's curse** [@Ioannidis2008].





::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true" code-summary="Code for the figure"}
set.seed(3)
G <- 2000; m <- 20; true_effect <- 0.3
study <- function() {
  a <- matrix(rnorm(m * G), m); b <- matrix(rnorm(m * G, true_effect), m)
  d <- colMeans(b) - colMeans(a)
  s <- sqrt((apply(a, 2, var) + apply(b, 2, var)) / 2)
  list(effect = d, t = d / (s * sqrt(2 / m)))
}
discovery <- study(); replication <- study()
top <- order(-discovery$t)[1:20]

par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(discovery$effect, replication$effect, pch = 19, cex = 0.4, col = "grey75", las = 1, asp = 1,
     xlab = "estimated effect in discovery", ylab = "estimated effect in replication")
abline(0, 1, lty = 2); abline(h = true_effect, v = true_effect, col = "#1F4E79", lty = 3)
points(discovery$effect[top], replication$effect[top], pch = 19, col = "#D35400")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![2,000 genes, all with the same true effect of 0.3 standard deviations, measured in a discovery study and an independent replication with 20 samples per group. The 20 genes with the largest discovery t-statistics (orange) have an estimated effect of about 1 in the discovery data, but about 0.4 in the replication. They were selected partly for their luck, and the luck does not replicate.](02-design_files/figure-html/fig-winners-curse-1.png){#fig-winners-curse width=576}
:::
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
c(true_effect = true_effect,
  top20_in_discovery   = mean(discovery$effect[top]),
  top20_in_replication = mean(replication$effect[top]))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>          true_effect   top20_in_discovery top20_in_replication 
#>             0.300000             1.051442             0.402163
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# replicates per group for 80% power: on the discovery estimate, and on the truth
c(planned_on_discovery = power.t.test(power = 0.8, delta = mean(discovery$effect[top]))$n,
  needed_for_truth     = power.t.test(power = 0.8, delta = true_effect)$n)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> planned_on_discovery     needed_for_truth 
#>             15.22211            175.38510
```


:::
:::





A replication powered on the discovery estimate would use about 15 samples per group and have very little power for an effect that is really 0.3. The consequence for design: power a confirmation on a deliberately conservative effect size, and treat a failed replication of an exploratory finding as the expected outcome rather than a surprise.

::: column-margin
**KEY** — Effects chosen because they look largest are overestimated. Plan the confirmation on a smaller effect than the discovery suggests.
:::

::: column-margin
**↪** Day 9 meets the same phenomenon after variable selection with the lasso: refitting the selected variables gives *p*-values that are too small.
:::

### Write down the choices

An exploratory analysis is allowed to be flexible, but each choice (the normalisation, which genes to filter, the distance measure, the number of clusters, which outliers to drop) is an opportunity to make the result look better. Trying many and reporting the most convincing is multiple testing in disguise, sometimes called the *garden of forking paths* [@Gelman2014]. Three habits keep this honest: fix the preprocessing before looking at the outcome; keep the validation labels hidden until the analysis plan is final; and keep a log of what was tried, so that the report can say how many paths were explored.

### Prediction: design for where the model will be used

A predictive model is judged by its error on new cases, so the test data should resemble those cases. A classifier developed on biopsies from one hospital, with half of the patients diseased, will meet a different prevalence, a different scanner or sequencer and a different patient mix when it is used elsewhere. The design questions are therefore about the **target population**: which hospitals, which time period, which prevalence. An **external validation** set from another centre or a later period is the most convincing test. And a model cannot be more accurate than its labels: if the "truth" in the training data comes from a noisy diagnosis, that noise is part of the design too.

### Integration: one design vocabulary, three kinds of question

| Design question | Confirm | Explore | Predict |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| What comes first? | the hypothesis | the data | the outcome to predict |
| What makes the conclusion honest? | randomisation, a fixed $\alpha$ | replication on independent data | a locked test set, external validation |
| Nuisance variation | keep small, block | sample broadly, record | match the target population |
| Experimental unit | sets the degrees of freedom | sets the unit of the split | sets the unit of the split |
| Batches | block, randomise | balance groups over batches | balance; test on new batches |
| Sample size | power for a stated effect | rare groups, stability, a pilot | precision of the error rate |
| Allowed claim | "causes" (if randomised) | "suggests", "worth testing" | "predicts, with this error, here" |

The vocabulary of the first half of the chapter is needed in every column. What changes is what it protects. In a confirmatory study it protects the test from bias; in a data-driven study it protects the patterns from being artefacts, and the honest check from having been used up before it was made.

## Key takeaways

- First decide what kind of question the study asks. In **confirmatory** research the hypothesis selects the data; in **exploratory** research the data select the hypothesis; in **prediction** the aim is a low error on new cases. Each licenses a different claim.
- The leverage over a study is spent before data collection. Design determines quality; analysis can only reveal it.
- Write the model first. It states what is to be measured, in what type, and where variance will enter, and it becomes the spreadsheet header.
- Partition the variance into named sources. SSH is signal; SSM and SSU are the dangerous terms that can violate assumptions or masquerade as signal.
- Use the four levers deliberately: **control** to make comparisons interpretable, **randomise** what cannot be controlled, **replicate** at the level of the experimental unit, and **block** what can be identified.
- Identify the experimental unit correctly. Counting sample units instead of experimental units is pseudoreplication, and it manufactures false confidence.
- Keep type I and type II error distinct. Fix $\alpha$; maximise power. Every reduction in $\sigma$ purchases power at no cost. Compute the required sample size *a priori*, with `power.t.test` or by simulation.
- A hypothesis cannot be tested on the data that suggested it. When the data come first, plan the independent check (a locked validation set or a replication cohort) before the study starts, and size it.
- Balance biological groups over batches, record all metadata, and power a confirmation on a conservative effect size: discovered effects are overestimated.

## Looking ahead

The dependencies you learned to *recognise* in this lecture, rats in boxes, pieces of a liver, samples in sequencing runs, are the structures that decide on Day 7 how data may be resampled and split. Design and resampling are two halves of one skill: identifying correlation, then respecting it.

The three kinds of question organise the rest of the course. Days 4 and 5 explore: PCA and clustering will always return directions and groups, and Exercise 2.1 showed why those are hypotheses rather than results. Day 6 returns to models and likelihood, and from Day 7 onwards the question is prediction, where Exercise 2.2 returns as cross-validation and the rule that every data-driven choice belongs inside the loop. The simulation skill of this chapter is the bridge throughout: set a known truth, generate data around it, and observe what the analysis recovers.

Two questions should precede every real measurement: *has the true experimental unit been identified, and are there enough of them to detect the effect of interest?* For a data-driven study a third joins them: *where will the independent data come from?* Answering these in advance is what makes a post mortem unnecessary.
